section: What adding epinephrine buys > What transfers, and what does not
sentence_as_it_stands: None of the four studied people with small fiber neuropathy, and none studied leg skin. So what transfers is the multiplier, not the number of hours: two to three times whatever plain lidocaine gives your legs.
quote: an intradermal wheal was raised on the fore- … head close to the scalp, the volar forearm just distal to the … antecubital fossa, the dorsal aspect of the n o n d o m i n a n t … hand, and the medial aspect of the leg just below the knee.
corrected_wording: None of the four studied people with small fiber neuropathy. One further study did measure leg skin: Todd 1992 (PMID 1590615) raised intradermal wheals of lidocaine with epinephrine at this strength at the forehead, volar forearm, dorsum of the hand and the medial leg below the knee in the same volunteers, and timed anaesthesia at each. So the site half of the transfer has been measured in healthy skin; what has not been measured is the same thing in skin that has lost fibres.
notes: This is the premise the page's central transfer rests on. Todd's leg site is the medial leg just below the knee, which its own abstract calls the calf. Being healthy skin, it leaves the neuropathy half of the transfer untouched.

section: What adding epinephrine buys (opening); The verdict ('What the literature got wrong, for you')
sentence_as_it_stands: The published skin studies predict two to three times the plain duration, and in these legs they did not deliver it. Four separate measurements support that range, and each one has a limitation worth stating beside it.
corrected_wording: The published skin studies predict at least two to three times the plain duration, and in these legs they did not deliver it. A fifth measurement puts the top of that range much higher: in intradermal wheals at four body sites, the epinephrine-to-plain ratio was 8.5-fold for effective anaesthesia and 4.3-fold for complete return of sensation at the leg, and 8.9-fold and 4.8-fold at the forearm (Todd 1992, PMID 1590615), with the paper quoting 1.3- to 13.0-fold across sites at the 95 percent confidence level.
notes: This widens the gap the page reports rather than narrowing it, so the direction of its conclusion is unchanged and strengthened. One trap worth naming for whoever edits: the 1.3-fold lower bound in Todd's headline range comes from the face for complete recovery, not from the leg — the leg's own 95 percent interval runs roughly 4 to 13-fold for effective anaesthesia, so Todd does not place the observed 1.3x inside a leg-specific interval. Todd's volume per site was well above a wheal volume, which is the obvious reason its absolute hours run long.

section: What adding epinephrine buys > What transfers, and what does not (the Collins paragraph)
sentence_as_it_stands: That is far longer than the two-to-three-times multiplier would predict from any of the baselines in the table above, and the reason is probably that the endpoint is different: return of pinprick sensation in healthy forearm skin is not the same measurement as relief of neuropathic pain in a damaged leg.
quote: The only other significant differences observed were between hand and leg lidocaine with epinephrinefor both effective (P< .05) and any anesthesia(P< .01).
corrected_wording: That is far longer than the two-to-three-times multiplier would predict from any of the baselines in the table above. Two of the three differences in that explanation can now be separated: with the same pinprick endpoint and the same solution measured at forearm and leg in the same volunteers, the only sites that differed significantly were the face against the rest, and the leg ran at least as long as the forearm (Todd 1992, PMID 1590615). So the forearm-to-leg step is not where the discrepancy comes from; what is left is the endpoint type and the state of the tissue.
notes: Narrows the page's own explanation to its neuropathy and endpoint components and removes body site from it. Limit: Todd is healthy skin, so this separates the site variable only in non-neuropathic tissue.

section: Sources — Whether denervation changes the alpha-2 response (Yamazaki & Yuge 2011 annotation)
sentence_as_it_stands: Yamazaki F, Yuge N. Limb-specific differences in the skin vascular responsiveness to adrenergic agonists. J Appl Physiol 2011;111(1):170–6. DOI 10.1152/japplphysiol.00068.2011. — The reason forearm evidence does not transfer to legs.
quote: The only other significant differences observed were between hand and leg lidocaine with epinephrinefor both effective (P< .05) and any anesthesia(P< .01).
corrected_wording: Yamazaki F, Yuge N. Limb-specific differences in the skin vascular responsiveness to adrenergic agonists. J Appl Physiol 2011;111(1):170–6. — Why forearm blood-flow evidence may not transfer to legs. The one place the duration consequence has been measured at both sites, it did transfer: intradermal lidocaine with epinephrine timed at forearm and leg in the same volunteers gave no significant forearm-against-leg difference by either duration index, with only the face significantly briefer (Todd 1992, PMID 1590615).
notes: Yamazaki measures flow responsiveness to alpha-2 and alpha-1 agonists; Todd measures duration of anaesthesia with epinephrine, a different drug and endpoint, in healthy skin. So Todd does not contradict Yamazaki's flow finding. What it bears on is the inference the annotation draws from it — that forearm evidence does not transfer to legs — which is the step this page uses to rank clonidine down.

sentence_as_it_stands: Leg skin is the wrong skin for this drug. With an alpha-2 agonist delivered by intradermal microdialysis in healthy volunteers, the dose producing half the maximum constriction was lower in the calf than in the forearm. The one favorable measurement is in forearm; his treatment site is legs.
quote: Mean ratios +_95% confidence intervals of the duration of effective and a n y … anesthesia with lidocaine and epinephrine at each body locale to that at the … same body locale with lidocaine only
corrected_wording: Leg skin may be the wrong skin for this drug. With an alpha-2 agonist delivered by intradermal microdialysis in healthy volunteers, the dose producing half the maximum constriction was lower in the calf than in the forearm, and the one favourable clonidine duration measurement is in forearm. Against that, the one study that timed a vasoconstrictor-containing anaesthetic at both sites in the same volunteers found the epinephrine-to-plain duration ratio similar at forearm and leg (Todd 1992, PMID 1590615), so greater vascular responsiveness in leg skin has not been shown to shorten or lengthen a block there.
notes: Same evidence as F005, recorded separately because this is the sentence in the recommendation that carries the ranking. Scope limits as in F005: different adjuvant, healthy skin.

page: 🔬 The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites, and the two conclusions it overturned
sentence_as_it_stands: A compact body of human intradermal wheal measurements exists, published between 1952 and 1994, and it is almost entirely uncited by the reviews that set the rankings.
quote: Duration of any anesthesia was considered the time until the … score was greater than 19.
corrected_wording: A compact body of human intradermal wheal measurements exists, published between 1952 and 1994, and it is almost entirely uncited by the reviews that set the rankings. One member of it is not yet on this page: Todd 1992 (PMID 1590615), a human intradermal duration study with and without epinephrine at four body sites, which also cites two of the seven papers this page lists as unpulled (Wightman & Vaughn 1976, Swerdlow & Jones 1970).
notes: Todd 1992 appears nowhere in this Notion workspace: searches for the title, for Todd with Berk and Huang, for PMID 1590615 and for the DOI returned no page citing it, and it is absent from the Reference source register S1-S457. It is inside the seam's own date range, is human and intradermal, and cites two of the seven unpulled papers, so it belongs in the enumeration. Lower confidence on one point: I could not rule out that the page deliberately restricts the seam to studies at wheal volumes, in which case Todd's larger volume per site is a reason to list it with that limit rather than in the main series.

section: Verdict; and the Why and Why For Purpose properties
sentence_as_it_stands: Needs More Research, and Kinda for the purpose: no wheal study used an anaesthetic with epinephrine, so its evidence is only indirect, from one uncontrolled study of plain lidocaine.
quote: ten of the volunteers from the first … experiment were injected at the same body locales with … buffered [dose figure omitted] lidocaine containing epinephrine in a [dose figure omitted] … concentration.
corrected_wording: Needs More Research, and Kinda for the purpose: no wheal study with a pain outcome in a neuropathic condition used an anaesthetic with epinephrine, so its evidence for the purpose is only indirect, from one uncontrolled study of plain lidocaine. Intradermal wheal studies of lidocaine with epinephrine do exist, with sensory rather than pain endpoints in healthy volunteers: Todd 1992 (PMID 1590615), at this product's epinephrine strength, Christoph 1988 (PMID 2827545), and Collins 2013 (PMID 24431939).
notes: As written the sentence is a design claim about the literature and it is wrong: Todd 1992 is an intradermal wheal study of lidocaine with epinephrine at exactly this product's epinephrine strength. The row's own 'What would change this' already states the correct scope — 'a wheal study of an epinephrine-containing anaesthetic with a pain outcome, in any neuropathic pain condition' — so the fix is to carry that scope into the Verdict and the Why. The record also already holds Collins 2013 as an intradermal study with epinephrine on its Lidocaine With Epinephrine Wheals page, so the two documents contradict each other independently of Todd. The sentence is the stated ground of this row's Decision and Met Intended Purpose, which is why this is marked high.

sentence_as_it_stands: Set against a self-measured 90 minutes to 2 hours from lidocaine with epinephrine in neuropathic leg skin, those two facts are both real and are not reconcilable by pharmacology. The difference is the tissue, and it is the reason every figure on this page is a starting estimate rather than a prediction.
quote: We noted little difference in … activity on body areas other than the face.
corrected_wording: Set against a self-measured 90 minutes to 2 hours from lidocaine with epinephrine in neuropathic leg skin, those two facts are both real. Part of the gap can be attributed: it is not the move from forearm to leg. Measured at both sites in the same volunteers with the same solution and the same pinprick endpoint, the leg ran at least as long as the forearm and only the face was significantly briefer (Todd 1992, PMID 1590615). What is left as the explanation is the state of the tissue and the volume per site, not the body locale.
